business.title: Complex social dominance behavior using a novel platform test is associated with lateral habenula activation in male and female mice
business.desc: Social hierarchy influences behavior, resource access, and health, but the neural mechanisms underlying individual differences in social competition remain incompletely understood. Using a novel competitive platform test and assessment of region-specific activation in male and female mice, we found a range of social hierarchies as determined by time on platform, revealing greater behavioral complexity than previously described and improved stability in females. We also measured motivated behavior and saw reduced platform acquisition attempts over testing days as well as rank-dependent differences in platform co-occupancy, which were seen primarily amongst lower ranks. We found no association between rank and medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC) activation, but found a positive correlation between lateral habenula (LHb) activation and rank. Social dominance was magnified in a group setting compared to paired matchups with similar motivation and co-occupancy behavior between ranks. There was no association between rank and mPFC activation in a group setting, but the LHb was again positively correlated with rank. Collectively, these findings demonstrate that the competitive platform task captures individual differences in social competition, motivation, and resource-sharing behavior under an aversive stimulus and identify the LHb as a neural correlate of performance in this behavioral context. These results highlight the complexity of social interactions in both sexes and provide insight into neural mechanisms that contribute to competitive social behavior.

technology.title: Wafer-scale porous graphene network shows room-temperature ferromagnetism
technology.desc: Researchers at Shenzhen University, the Japan Atomic Energy Agency, the National Institutes for Quantum Science and Technology (QST), the University of Tokyo, the University of Science and Technology of China, Xi'an Jiaotong University, Shenzhen Technology University (SZTU), and The Hong Kong Polytechnic University, have grown a wafer-scale hyper-porous graphene network (HGN) that shows intrinsic ferromagnetism at room temperature. Optical image of HGN on a 2-inch Si wafer. Image from: NanowerkThe film was produced across a full 2-inch oxide-coated silicon wafer using a plasma-assisted vapor process combined with low-energy electron irradiation, and reached a magnetic moment density roughly 1,000 times higher than defected highly oriented pyrolytic graphite (HOPG). Unlike a conventional graphene film, the HGN's layers stand roughly perpendicular to the substrate and curve, split, and crosslink into a three-dimensional mesh riddled with pores smaller than about 2 nm. Atomic-resolution transmission electron microscopy revealed that these pores expose abundant zigzag graphene edges, many of them separated by more than roughly 1.4 nm. The same deposition setup, run under different conditions, also produced an amorphous carbon film with a much more disordered atomic arrangement and no comparable network of exposed edges, giving the researchers a directly comparable control material made in the same growth environment.At room temperature, the porous network reached a saturation magnetization of 4.7 emu/g, more than three orders of magnitude above the graphite reference, corresponding to a magnetic moment of about 0.06 μB per carbon atom from bulk magnetometry. To rule out the usual culprit behind claims of magnetic carbon, trace magnetic contamination, the team used X-ray magnetic circular dichroism (XMCD) tuned to the carbon absorption edge, which reversed sign as expected when the magnetic field or X-ray polarization was reversed, while graphite and the amorphous carbon control showed no comparable signal. XMCD scans at the characteristic absorption energies of iron, cobalt, and nickel detected none of their signatures, and mass spectrometry showed that trace magnetic impurities in the sample could account for at most about 0.23% of the measured magnetization.

world.title: KENYA: Prelate Challenges Franciscans to be “Examples, Not Burdens to Others”
world.desc:
Sr. Jecinter Antoinette Okoth, FSSA
At the opening of a three-day Franciscan Jubilee symposium on Wednesday, August 26, at the Catholic University of Eastern Africa (CUEA), Franciscans from various congregations across Kenya were encouraged to be living examples of Christ to the people they serve, rather than “a spiritual, pastoral, liturgical, or economic burden” to them.
Addressing the congregation in his homily during the Eucharistic celebration, Archbishop Maurice Muhatia Makumba urged the Franciscans to examine how faithfully they are living out the charism of St. Francis of Assisi in their various ministries: education, health, social work, catechesis and pastoral care.
Let us pray to God that none of us may become a burden to the people to whom we have been sent, the Archbishop said, adding that Franciscans everywhere are called instead to be among them examples to emulate.
The symposium organized by the Franciscan Family Association- Kenya was themed, Lord Make Me an Instrument of Your Peace, in response to the pressing lack of peace in the world today, including “conflicts in the Middle East, Gaza, Ukraine and Congo, tribalism within African countries including Kenya, xenophobia, environmental destruction, and instability within families, religious institutions and governments.”
Archbishop Muhatia of Kisumu Archdiocese referring to his own journey with the Franciscan family, tracing it from his home diocese of Kakamega in Kenya, where Franciscan presence was minimal, to the Diocese of Nakuru, where he served for over 12 years, and found himself immersed among numerous Franciscan congregations, both male and female, recalled that being surrounded wherever he turned,  by the  Franciscan communities has deepened his Franciscan spirituality  adding that even in the Archdiocese he currently he serves.
Reflecting on 16 years as a bishop shaped by this intense encounter with Franciscan missionaries, he said his life story would be completely impoverished without the Franciscan witness woven through it and thanked the gathered religious for their impact on his ministry.
Archbishop Muhatia, who is also the chairman of the Kenya Conference of Catholic Bishops (KCCB), urged the assembled religious to examine themselves as to whether they had promoted the charism of their institutes, remained faithful to their superiors, served those they were sent to serve, or allowed themselves to grow lukewarm.
The Archbishop found encouragement in St. Paul's boldness in inviting the Thessalonians to imitate him and his companions, not because of their perfection, but because of their fidelity to the responsibility entrusted to them.
St Paul's insistence that he and his companions worked night and day so as not to burden anyone, the Archbishop said, offers a model for Franciscan life today: ministry offered generously, without becoming a weight on the people served.
The three-day event at CUEA brought together members of the First, Second and Third Orders, both Regular and Secular Franciscans, together with institutes of consecrated life, societies of apostolic life, and public and private associations of the faithful who live by the Rule of St. Francis or draw inspiration from his spirituality.
The Franciscan symposium forms part of wider celebrations marking the Jubilee Year of St. Francis of Assisi, proclaimed by Pope Leo XIV on the occasion of the 8th centenary of St. Francis’ death. The Jubilee runs from January 10, 2026, to January 10, 2027.

world.title: CUEA: Welcomes New Rector and Vice-Chancellor, Rev. Prof. Elias Opongo, SJ
world.desc:
Stephen Mbobu
A new chapter has begun at the Catholic University of Eastern Africa (CUEA) with the assumption of office by Rev. Prof. Elias Omondi Opongo, SJ, as the University’s new Rector and Vice-Chancellor, effective Tuesday, 1st September 2026.
His appointment follows the conclusion of the tenure of the immediate former Vice-Chancellor, Very Rev. Prof. Stephen Mbugua Ngari, whose term ended on 31st August 2026 following an elaborate and orderly handover process.
The transition ceremony, preceded by Holy Mass, brought together members of the University community and key stakeholders to mark the leadership transition.
In his remarks, the Chair of the University Council, Rt. Rev. Mark Kadima, Bishop of the Catholic Diocese of Bungoma, challenged the incoming Vice-Chancellor to embrace the call of the day’s Scripture readings by remaining available, reliable, and persevering, particularly during challenging moments.
Drawing from Luke 4:18–19, which echoes the prophetic words of Isaiah (Is. 61:1-2), Bishop Kadima reminded the new Vice-Chancellor of Christ’s mission:
“The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me to bring glad tidings to the poor. He has sent me to proclaim liberty to captives and recovery of sight to the blind, to let the oppressed go free, and to proclaim a year acceptable to the Lord.”
He also called upon CUEA staff and the wider University community to give maximum support and cooperation to the incoming Vice-Chancellor as he takes up the responsibility of leading the institution.
Most Rev. Philip Anyolo, Archbishop of Nairobi and Pro-Chancellor of CUEA, witnessed the occasion and commended all parties for ensuring a very orderly transition. He expressed appreciation to the outgoing Vice-Chancellor for his leadership, particularly in steering the University through a period of successful recovery.
Also present were Rev. Fr. Andrew Kaufa, the new AMECEA Secretary General and member of the CUEA Council; Deputy Vice-Chancellors; University Executive Directors; the Legal Officer; and other members of the University leadership.
As CUEA welcomes its new Rector and Vice-Chancellor, the University community looks forward to a new season of faith-filled leadership, academic excellence, innovation, service, and renewed institutional growth.
